alt: Giddens defines globalisation as the intensification of worldwide social relations that shape local events and vice versa; Harvey describes time-space compression. Answers can separate flows of people, goods, money, images and ideas from the structures that manage them.
caption: Say what changes: intensifying links and compressed time and space.

alt: Appadurai’s five scapes, ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, financescapes and ideoscapes, each with what flows and an example of a disjuncture between them.
caption: Uneven flows mean global culture is not simply Westernisation.

alt: A timeline of global political norms: the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights, CEDAW in 1979, Fukuyama in 1989, the Beijing Platform in 1995 and the International Criminal Court from 2002, with a note that norms are unevenly enforced.
caption: Global norms are widely signed but selectively practised.

after: ## How far has globalisation gone? The extent debate
alt: Hyperglobalist, sceptical (Hirst and Thompson) and transformationalist views of how far globalisation has gone, with a reminder to judge capital, labour, culture and political norms separately.
caption: Capital is global; people are not.

after: ## Who has gained and who has lost?
alt: A schematic elephant-shaped curve of income gains from 1988 to 2008 across the global income distribution: the largest gains in the global middle, mostly in Asia, and the richest 1 per cent, and the smallest gains among the lower-middle classes of rich countries.
caption: Globalisation’s gains were unequal, which explains both support and resentment.

after: ## The global and the local: how the local survives
alt: Four ways global and local interact: Robertson’s glocalisation, Ritzer’s grobalisation, Nederveen Pieterse’s hybridisation and Barber’s resistance and revival, with an exam tip on distinct mechanisms.
caption: The local adapts, mixes and pushes back as well as being standardised.
